listings.name: Seattle CityPASS
listings.content: A discount pass that includes admission to five attractions for half the normal fee combined. You are entitled to up to two visits (within 24 hours) to the Space Needle and a visit to the Seattle Aquarium. You also get three choices of an Argosy Cruises Harbor Tour, admission to the Museum of Pop Culture, the Woodland Park Zoo, the Pacific Science Center the Museum of Flight, or Chihuly Garden & Glass. A CityPASS is valid for 9 consecutive days starting with the use of your first ticket. Transportation and parking are not included.
listings.price: $127 for adult, $97 for children (ages 5-12), plus tax and a $2 processing fee per ticket

listings.name: Kenmore Air
listings.content: 20 minute plane tours over Seattle that are narrated by the pilot, with spectacular views of the city. Tours begin and end at the west side of Lake Union. Reservations required.

listings.name: Argosy Cruises
listings.content: Boat tour company with special dinner and sightseeing cruises. The most common tour is the hour-long Harbor Cruise on Elliott Bay, which offers excellent views of the Space Needle, Downtown skyline, freight harbor, and usually some sea lions, with a barrage of informative commentary about local history or interesting ships or cargo passing through that day. The Locks Cruise is a 2-hour one-way trip (in alternating directions) through the locks separating Elliot Bay and Lake Union, with an optional bus ride if you prefer a round trip. Seasonal cruises include the Summer Views Cruise with a sunset on Puget Sound, and Husky Football Cruises on Lake Washington before the games. Most cruises offer a decent full-service bar with large drinks and some snacks.
listings.price: Harbor cruise $30.50. Locks cruise $42.50, bus connection $5 additional. Discounts for kids 4-12 and seniors

listings.name: Waterways Cruises
listings.content: Luxury dining cruises touring Lake Union and Lake Washington. Regular cruises include 2-hour weekend brunch and Sunday supper buffets, and a 2½-hour four-course dinner (business casual attire).

listings.name: Chinese Lunar New Year
listings.content: Numerous stalls and performances, and don't forget to partake in all the cheap food!

listings.name: Seattle International Film Festival
listings.content: One of the largest film festivals in North America, showing international cinema. Watch indie films at Seattle area screens and vote for your favorite; each category winner receives a Golden Space Needle trophy. SIFF also screens films year-round at its venues.

listings.name: Northwest Folklife Festival
listings.content: A more low-key and local version of Bumbershoot, mainly family-friendly.
listings.price: Free ($10 donation per person per day encouraged)

listings.name: Fremont Fair
listings.content: Home of the Solstice Parade (including the nude bike ride), and a really fun drunken time all over Fremont. Vendors, bad live music and eclectic crowds at the bars make for an interesting time. Friends who live in Fremont become especially valuable for a place to crash during the fair.

listings.name: Seattle PrideFest
listings.content: One of the biggest gay pride festivals in the country. Food carts, beer gardens, adult theme performances, and the eagerly anticipated Pride Parade.

listings.name: Bite of Seattle
listings.content: Part of Seafair festivities. Enjoy some of the best delicacies of Seattle.

listings.name: Capitol Hill Block Party
listings.content: Yearly live music event held on Capitol Hill over a weekend in mid-summer (usually the end of July). Consists primarily of local independent bands of various styles, coupled with some bigger name independent label acts.

listings.name: Seafair
listings.content: Seattle's biggest festival, signifying the arrival of summer. Neighborhood events such as parades and street fairs run throughout the festival, with the downtown Torchlight Parade in late July. Seafair culminates in early August when hydroplane races and the Blue Angels bring loud, fast boats and planes to Lake Washington.

listings.name: Bumbershoot
listings.content: Seattle's largest music and arts festival, featuring dozens of local and world-class musical acts.

listings.name: Night Market & Autumn Moon Festival
listings.content: Chinese festival of food and outdoor market.

listings.name: Luminata
listings.content: A festival of lights at Green Lake, including a procession from the old Aqua Theatre to a clearing about 3/4 mile north.

listings.name: Festál Cultural Center
listings.content: Celebrate the world with festivals from about 25 countries represented, one country nearly every 2 weeks.

listings.name: Hiram M. Chittenden Locks
listings.content: Linking the freshwater Lake Union and the salt-water Puget Sound across a height difference of 22 feet, the locks allow boats to cross the Lake Washington Ship Canal, relying solely on the force of gravity. A salmon ladder with a viewing gallery allows visitors to witness the salmon migration, which with different species allow for viewing throughout most of the year, but preferably mid to late summer. Adjacent is the Carl S English, Jr Botanical Garden. Guided tours weekdays 1PM and 3PM; weekends 11AM.
listings.image: Lake Washington ship canal, Hiram M. Chittenden Locks, 1995.jpg

listings.name: National Nordic Museum
listings.content: Documents the history of Scandinavian immigration to Seattle, with rotating art exhibits and a permanent collection of historical artifacts. Julefest includes discounted admission and a Christmas market.
listings.price: $20 adults, $16 seniors, $15 college students, $10 children above 5 yrs, under 5 free

listings.name: Edith Macefield "Up" House
listings.content: Edith Macefield received worldwide attention in 2006 when she turned down an offer of $1 million to sell her house to make way for a five-story commercial development. Instead, the Ballard Blocks project was built surrounding her 108-year-old farmhouse. While production of the film Up, based on a strikingly similar premise, started two years before, Disney acknowledged the story with a promotional tie-in.

listings.name: Ballard Commons Park
listings.content: Ballard Commons Park features a playground, skate bowl, water feature, engaging public art, relaxing seating areas and lawns and ADA accessible walkways.

listings.name: Golden Gardens Park
listings.content: A wonderful saltwater beach park in Ballard, past the locks and Shilshole Marina. Water around here is too cold to swim except for crazy and determined kids during the hottest months, but you can wade a little, walk the beach, make sand castles, claim a fire pit, and watch wind surfers and ships go by. On clear days there is a magnificent view of the Olympics on the other side of Puget Sound. Kids of all ages have endless muddy fun trying to dam up or re-route the fresh water stream flowing across one end of the beach.

listings.name: Greenlake Park
listings.content: The focal point of the Green Lake neighborhood. The 2.8 loop path around the lake is frequented by cyclists, runners, rollerbladers, and walkers. The lake is swimmer friendly; algae growth and closures were sometimes a problem before 2004, when the City of Seattle performed a comprehensive cleanup, and it is now one of the cleanest public swimming areas in the Seattle area.

listings.name: Sacred Rain Healing Center
listings.content: Connect with yourself. Seattle's only indoor/outdoor, all-gender clothing-optional hydrotherapy spa. Therapeutic massage, acupuncture, chiropractic, naturopathic physician, yoga, sacred music, nature-bathing. 18 and older.

listings.name: Greenwood Classic Car Show
listings.content: Outdoor car show with all types of cars and food vendors about 1 mile along Greenwood Ave North.

listings.name: Ballard Seafoodfest
listings.content: A parade, a salmon barbecue, local musicians and a lutefisk-eating contest. Most businesses along NW Market St participate by holding sidewalk sales.

listings.name: Greenwood/Phinney Art Walk
listings.content: Showcases hundreds of local artists.

listings.name: Julefest
listings.content: Discounted admission to the Nordic Museum and a large collection of food, drink, and craft vendors, with live music. A Nordic-inspired Christmas market.

listings.name: Freakout Festival
listings.content: An annual 4-day underground music festival held at various venues around the neighborhood each November.

listings.name: Conor Byrne Pub
listings.content: A small live music venue and bar.

listings.name: Tractor Tavern
listings.content: A medium-sized live music venue typically only open during shows

listings.name: Sunset Tavern
listings.content: A small live music venue and bar.

listings.name: Egan's Ballard Jam House
listings.content: A small intimate music supper club with mostly jazz (vocal and instrumental) and other styles of live music offered. Open mic (vocal jam) every other Wednesday evening.

listings.name: Bad Albert's Tap & Grill
listings.content: Cheap yet good quality pub grub: burgers, excellent fries, hot sandwiches, soups and salads.

listings.name: Gordito's Healthy Mexican Food
listings.content: Huge servings, a fast but sometimes long line, way-cheap prices, amazingly tasty burritos that most folks can't finish in one sitting (the "Baby burrito" is about the size of an actual baby), lots of homemade salsas (on the salsa bar), and an outdoor patio.

listings.name: Larsen's Danish Bakery
listings.content: Famous throughout Seattle, this is the best Scandinavian-style bakery in town.

listings.name: Mike's Chili Parlor
listings.content: Located just east of the Ballard bridge, this combination dive tavern/chili parlor is a good place to grab a spicy, cheap meal. They do chili burgers and dogs too. Cash only!

listings.name: Red Mill Burgers
listings.content: Good old-fashioned burgers, fries, and shakes with both indoor and outdoor seating. Cash or card, closed Mondays.

listings.name: El Moose
listings.content: Authentic Mexican cooking from Mexico. Try the pork carnitas.

listings.name: Taquería Tequila Authentic Mexican Food
listings.content: The name might be deceiving, but this place takes its Mexican food just as seriously as it takes being a place to drink. Cheap burritos, tacos, quesadillas, fajitas.

listings.name: Valhalla Sandwiches
listings.content: Features tasty sandwiches, tots, beer and cider.

listings.name: La Carta de Oaxaca
listings.content: Cheap and good Oaxaca-style Mexican food.

listings.name: Indian Bistro
listings.content: Reasonably priced and delicious. Friendly owner and a definite go-to for any Indian food lover.

listings.name: Lockspot Cafe
listings.content: This is an old breakfast and lunch (burgers, mostly) spot that's mostly patronized by local workers and very popular with them.

listings.name: Matador
listings.content: Somewhat pricier, more upscale Tex-Mex fare, though their happy-hour bar food menu is more reasonable.

listings.name: Delancey
listings.content: New York-style pizza that rivals anything you could find in New York city. Delancey is the product of NY transplants and its attention to detail shows. The menu is simple and well executed, basically just pizza and salad.

listings.name: Ridge Pizza
listings.content: Neighborhood pizza joint. Pizza varieties named after local shops and restaurants.

listings.name: Old Salt
listings.content: House-made bagels with in-house smoked fish.

listings.name: Rachel's Bagels & Burritos
listings.content: House-made bagels, biscuits, and burritos.

listings.name: The Walrus and The Carpenter
listings.content: Excellent oyster bar in a restored historic building. No reservations; the wait is often 1-2 hours unless you get there very early. The adjacent Barnacle bar is a great place to wait while sipping Italian aperitif cocktails and antipasti.

listings.name: Rupee Bar
listings.content: Intimate bar presenting modern cocktails & small plates inspired by Sri Lanka & India.

listings.name: Copine
listings.content: Classic French technique meets local ingredients in a breezy, sophisticated space. Menu is typically prixe fixe only, with bar seating with a smaller menu.

listings.name: Ray's Boathouse and Ray's Cafe
listings.content: Great views and, in the downstairs Boathouse restaurant, some of the best seafood cooking in the city, priced accordingly. Upstairs, Ray's Cafe is more casual, the food is good but not comparable to the Boathouse downstairs.

listings.name: Jolly Roger/Maritime Pacific Brewing Company
listings.content: The Jolly Roger serves as the taproom for Maritime Pacific Brewing Company, the oldest brewery in Ballard, with upscale pub food, in-house beers & pirate-themed decor.

listings.name: Fair Isle Brewing
listings.content: Brewery and taproom specializing in lagers and mixed-culture saisons using farmed and foraged ingredients such as fireweed, raspberries, elderberries, madrone bark, etc. The brewery also has a restaurant with snacks, small plates, and mains with vegetarian, seafood, and meat options.

listings.name: Angry Beaver
listings.content: Said to be the only Canadian-themed bar in Seattle. Great poutine, perfect for hockey fanatics. Full bar.

listings.name: Prost!
listings.content: Great little Bavarian-style German pub loaded with great German beer and all beers served in their appropriate glassware.
listings.price: $5-6 for half a liter, $10-12 for a liter of beer

listings.name: Bleacher's
listings.content: Standard sports bar, stiff drinks.

listings.name: Gainsbourg
listings.content: French fare with great variety of wine, beer, cocktails, and absinthe.

listings.name: The Baranof
listings.content: Classic dive. A Greenwood institution. Go for the karaoke.

listings.name: Little Tin
listings.content: Cocktail bar with Tiki and Hawaiian-inspired drinks and snacks.

listings.name: Olaf's
listings.content: Relaxed neighborhood watering hole featuring a wide selection of draft beers & elevated bar bites. Two televisions usually showing sports.

listings.name: Old County Bar
listings.content: Sports bar with full bar, several beers on draft, one pool table and darts. Several televisions usually showing sports.

listings.name: Miro Tea
listings.content: A contemporary tea house with a large selection of beverages and food.

listings.name: Valentinas Cafe
listings.content: Delicious Mexican-inspired coffee and tea drinks and pastries in a whimsical, floral-themed space.

listings.name: Victrola Coffee Roasters
listings.content: Excellent spot to grab a drink, get a little work done, or peoplewatch at the popular corner of Market and 22nd.

listings.name: Venture Coffee Co
listings.content: Eco-conscious, counter-serve coffeehouse featuring varied fair-trade blends & light fare.

listings.name: Hotel Ballard
listings.content: Mediterranean-style hotel in the heart of Ballard. 29 rooms and suites with marble and carpet tiles in lavish rooms. It also hosts Stoneburner, an in-house pizzeria, in the lobby, and a rooftop pavilion. For pampering or sports, an athletic club with swimming pool, gym, and spa is just next door.

listings.name: Ballard Inn
listings.content: An updated inn with 16 small rooms, some with shared bathrooms.
listings.price: From $100 per night for room with a shared bathroom

listings.name: Greenlake Guest House
listings.content: A 4-room bed and breakfast overlooking Green Lake. The couple who own the place cook breakfast and constantly chat with guests.

listings.name: Northwest Nikkei Museum
listings.content: Small exhibits relating to the history of nikkei (Japanese immigrants) in the Pacific Northwest.

listings.name: Seattle Asian Art Museum
listings.content: An offshoot of downtown's Seattle Art Museum, SAAM displays a portion of the permanent collection balanced with rotating, consistently well-curated special exhibitions. The focus is usually on Chinese or Japanese art, reflecting long-established ties across the Pacific, but does include works from as far as India and the Middle East. The Art Deco building (the Seattle Art Museum's original home) is an attraction in its own right.
listings.price: $15/adult, $13/seniors, $13/military, $10/student, children free, last Fridays free, all tickets +$3 if not bought in advance

listings.name: Frye Art Museum
listings.content: A small private collection of modern art with rotating contemporary exhibitions. Parking is always available and the place is worth a visit.

listings.name: Cal Anderson Park
listings.content: A very popular park on sunny days. It includes a signature fountain and pond, a basketball court, tennis and softball fields, and a playground. Great for peoplewatching, and you can often see groups of people doing activities varying from hackeysack to drum circles to freeze tag to bike polo to twirling around with colorful scarves.

listings.name: Hot Rat Summer Mosaic
listings.content: A small tile-and-glass mosaic of a rat in a devotional pose, labeled with its namesake caption. It was illicitly installed on the side of a utility gatehouse in 2024. The city repeatedly tried to remove it, but community members swiftly striped away the paint covering it up amidst a swell of public appreciation for the art, so it was eventually allowed to stay.

listings.name: Lakeview Cemetery
listings.content: Incorporated in 1872, Lakeview Cemetery is set on a hillside with views of Lake Union, the Cascades, Lake Washington and the Olympic Mountains. The site holds the final resting places of Seattle's first families, many with diverse backgrounds. Many come to pay tribute at the graves of Bruce Lee and his son Brandon.

listings.name: Viretta Park
listings.content: The park's wooden benches are covered with graffiti messages to Nirvana frontman Kurt Cobain, as it is next door to the home where he died in 1994. This is the closest thing in Seattle to a memorial to the rock icon; serious fans should consider a road trip to his childhood hometown of Aberdeen.

listings.name: Volunteer Park
listings.content: Designed by John Charles Olmsted and Fredrick Law Olmsted Jr, this is the largest park in Capitol Hill. It is the site of a botanical conservatory and the Seattle Asian Art Museum (above).

listings.name: Volunteer Park Conservatory
listings.content: A Victorian-style greenhouse with thousands of living specimens on display. There are five sections: bromeliads, ferns, palms, seasonal, and cacti/succulents.
listings.price: Adult $6; Youth under 18, students, seniors 65+, military $4; children under 6 Free

listings.name: Water Tower
listings.content: The 1906 tower at the highest point of Capitol Hill has an observation deck at the top, with views from the Cascades to the Olympics interspersed with a series of panels explaining the history of Seattle's Olmsted-designed park system. The views are somewhat obstructed by metal grates, but the clever photographer can work around them. No elevator - the only way up is the staircase wound around the water tank, seven stories high.

listings.name: Washington Park Arboretum
listings.content: The Arboretum is a 230-acre park additionally serving as a botanical garden and horticultural research center, with thousands of trees and plants from temperate climates represented. An extensive network of walking trails covers the park. The visitor's center, near the northeast corner of the park, is open from 10AM to 4PM daily, and has limited parking available. Guided tours are offered on the first and third Sundays of every month, and free trail maps highlighting the major parts of the collection are available at any time.

listings.name: Seattle Japanese Garden
listings.content: A small, formal Japanese garden within the grounds of the Arboretum.
listings.price: $6 adults, $4 children over 5 years and seniors

listings.name: Streissguth Gardens
listings.content: A small, family-maintained garden on the northwest side of Seattle's Capitol Hill, on a steep hillside. Noisy but offering great views over Lake Union, Downtown Seattle, and the Olympic Mountains in the distance.
listings.address: E Blaine St between 10th Ave E and Broadway E
listings.image: Flickr - brewbooks - Mary Ellen at Streissguth Gardens - Seattle (2).jpg

listings.name: Madison Park
listings.content: Activities include swimming, bathhouse, restaurants, tennis court (with lights), and great views of the floating bridge and the Cascades. Lifeguards patrol the area during the summer, which creates a safer playground for kids, but it's still a beautiful park to hang out for teens and adults.

listings.name: Jimi Hendrix statue
listings.content: A life-size bronze sculpture of Hendrix rocks out on the sidewalk. Seattle was the birthplace and childhood home of the influential guitarist.

listings.name: Seattle University
listings.content: A private Jesuit university. Scenic campus makes a good walking detour.

listings.name: Chapel of St. Ignatius
listings.content: A hidden gem, this small campus chapel was described by architect Stephen Holl as "seven bottles of light in a stone box". It is probably the most notable religious building built in Seattle in the last fifty years.

listings.name: Hothouse Spa & Sauna
listings.content: A small urban women-only spa with an industrial/basement vibe. Great for a relaxing soak in the tub. Expect to be nude and quiet, and bring your own towels.

listings.name: Club Z
listings.content: On the other end of the spectrum, Club Z is a gay male bathhouse with no tubs and a lot of glory holes! Don't walk in if you expect to do any dancing or, um, bathing.

listings.name: Club Comedy Seattle
listings.content: Boutique style stand-up comedy club.

listings.name: Raygun Lounge
listings.content: All-ages gaming bar with board games and pinball machines. The atmosphere is more like a dive bar: the beer, cider and wine are good, but the food is mediocre, and the TVs are usually playing B-movies (but sometimes have some good campy sci-fi like Doctor Who).

listings.name: I-5 Colonnade Mountain Bike Skills Park
listings.content: The bike park was built underneath a section of 12 elevated lanes of Interstate 5. It consists of several mountain bike skills trails, including novice, intermediate, and advanced sections, a dirt jumping section, pump track, and trials area. Skills classes, organized by the Evergreen Mountain Bike Alliance, are occasionally held at the park.
listings.address: Lakeview Blvd E and Harvard Ave E

listings.name: Central Cinema
listings.content: A unique, smaller movie theater that shows older films as well as plenty of late night movie screenings of hilariously bad films. All seats have table in front of them so you can have excellent food and beer during the show. A couple times a month there are $1.99 movie nights for popular older or cult films.

listings.name: Northwest Film Forum
listings.content: A Seattle-based non-profit organization for film artists, showcasing American and international cinema as well as quarterly world premiere live performances.

listings.name: SIFF Cinema Egyptian
listings.content: One-screen theater showing art, indie, and foreign films and documentaries.

listings.name: Seattle International Film Festival (SIFF)
listings.content: One of the largest film festivals in North America. Screenings are at the SIFF Cinema Egyptian and other SIFF venues in adjacent districts.

listings.name: Capitol Hill Block Party
listings.content: This music festival during the height of summer attracts both local and national musicians.

listings.name: Big Mario's New York Pizza
listings.content: True New York-style thin crust pizza. Huge, foldable slices or whole pies. Full bar with lots of local beers. Pizza window open late night.

listings.name: Bakery Nouveau
listings.content: Everything you'd want from a French-style bakery: pastries, breads, elegant desserts, macarons, chocolate confections by the piece, sandwiches, quiches, and pizzas, plus coffee of course. Very popular; the line often stretches to the door and beyond, but it moves quickly enough. The limited seating is usually pretty full; in a pinch there's a park across the street with a bench of two.

listings.name: Dick's Drive-In
listings.content: Where the cool hang out (according to Sir Mix-a-Lot's song "Posse on Broadway"). Dick's is a local fast food staple; perhaps the most iconically "Seattle" restaurant around. The menu is simple: unsophisticated yet satisfying burgers in just a couple of variations (try the Deluxe, it's not that large), hot greasy fries, and tasty hand-dipped milkshakes. Drive up or walk up; this place will be hopping on a Friday or Saturday night, even if it's cold and rainy outside. Be sure to get in line by 1:45AM because they slam the order windows shut promptly at 2AM. Dick's cashiers have an amazing ability to instantly add up your bill in their head. There are other branches throughout the city (Lake City, Wallingford, Lower Queen Anne), but because the Capitol Hill one is easiest to walk up to, it's also the best for people watching.

listings.name: Ezell's Famous Chicken
listings.content: This Central District mainstay gained wide renown when Oprah Winfrey declared it her favorite, but it really needs no celebrity endorsements; it's hands-down the best stuff around. This flagship location sits directly across from Garfield High School. There's no seating, but they accept credit cards. Spicy and original; the spicy chicken isn't too spicy, but you can get a side of hot sauce for 11 cents extra. Daily specials vary based on forecasted surplus of unsold chicken.

listings.name: Frankie & Jo's
listings.content: Their coconut-based ice cream is decadently creamy and creatively flavored with seasonal ingredients.

listings.name: Hot Mama's Pizza
listings.content: Classic New York-style pizza by the slice. You can't go wrong here and the pesto is particularly popular.

listings.name: Italian Family Pizza
listings.content: Very good East Coast style pizza with large servings and cheap beer served all day in a restaurant operated by East Coast transplants. Relocated from downtown Seattle to a larger restaurant in First Hill.

listings.name: Jamjuree
listings.content: A Thai place that's fairly quiet and upscale, with excellent specials - try the Lime Light Chicken if you have a chance. On request they can make truly vegetarian Thai food (i.e., without fish sauce).

listings.name: Moonlight Cafe
listings.content: Serves excellent vegan mock-meat versions of Vietnamese and Chinese dishes such as noodle bowls and sesame beef. In fact, they boast a full vegan menu with as many dishes as their separate carnivorous menu offers.

listings.name: Ooink
listings.content: One of several excellent ramen shops in Capitol Hill. Depending on what style of ramen you prefer, you may like others such as Ramen Danbo, Betsutenjin, or Menya Musashi.

listings.name: Americana
listings.content: Eclectic menu of American fusion fare and some delicious simple cocktails. Extremely popular on weekends with their large brunch menu and Bloody Marys.

listings.name: Ayutthaya
listings.content: Inexpensive, quality Thai food. It specializes in Thai classics such as coconut chicken & drunken noodles, with happy hour.

listings.name: Ba Bar
listings.content: A myriad of cocktails plus Vietnamese street fare, which also includes a bakery. Known for its rotisserie meat, pho, banh cuon (rice noodle roll), and macaroons. Open late night with comfort food options. No reservations needed.

listings.name: Cactus
listings.content: A local favorite. A creative mix of Mexican, Southwestern and Spanish cuisine complemented by great cocktails. Always full, with outdoor seating in the summer.

listings.name: Cafe Flora
listings.content: Upscale, all-vegetarian cuisine in a casual atmosphere. Menus change weekly.

listings.name: Cafe Lago
listings.content: Established Italian restaurant popular for vegetarian lasagna, apple-wood fired pizza, and fresh hand-made pasta (they have an employee dedicated solely to making pasta). An excellent environment for families, they even have paper tablecloths for kids to draw on.

listings.name: Julia's On Broadway
listings.content: Julia's serves Northwest cuisine along with good ol' American food, breakfast, lunch and dinner. Average quality, expensive meals and cocktails are prepared in a charming old building that used to house a seriously divey gay bar until they gutted it and put in a tasteful interior. The location is excellent, but the service can be less than stellar. That's because the real attraction is not the food but the drag shows. Long-time residents decry the "loss" of a gay bar, but Julia's drag shows remain popular with tourists, bachelorette parties, and the like, particularly the weekend brunch shows.

listings.name: Monsoon
listings.content: Contemporary Vietnamese dishes (mainly southern Vietnamese) mixed with Pacific Northwest innovation. Dim sum brunches on the weekends.

listings.name: Pizzeria Pagliacci
listings.content: Serves unique Seattle-style pizza, reminiscent of thin-crust, by-the-slice New York pizza, but with an imaginative collection of toppings that change with the seasons. Walk in and ask for two slices of "primo" and you won't be disappointed. The Pagliaccio salad is a good starter. There are branches in the University District and Queen Anne, plus delivery throughout the city.

listings.name: Annapurna Cafe
listings.content: Perhaps the crown of Seattle's Indian food scene, Annapurna also serves excellent Nepali and Tibetan food. A charming atmosphere, quality food, and a wide variety of vegetarian and vegan options make it a great location for dinner.

listings.name: Cafe Soleil
listings.content: A casual and laid-back Ethiopian restaurant, serving both traditional Ethiopian food and adaptations using Northwest ingredients. Housed in a beautiful building with excellent natural light, with outdoor seating as well. Well-stocked with Ethiopian beers.

listings.name: Carrello
listings.content: Artisanal Italian food in small portions so you can construct a meal however you like. Carts roll past tables offering cheaper antipasti to supplement your meal or wash down your cocktail.

listings.name: Taneda
listings.content: Small Japanese bar serving prix fixe sushi in the style of kaiseki, a traditional multi-course meal consisting of several small dishes. Reservations required, and with only 17 seats and two dinners per night, they are booked up to 2 months in advance.

listings.name: Caffé Vita
listings.content: Coffee roaster with a warehouse feel, where patrons can clearly see how the coffee beans are roasted.

listings.name: Espresso Vivace Roasteria
listings.content: Founded by an engineer who's been developing progressively more sophisticated roasters for twenty years. Their beans, plus Mighty-O doughnuts, are also available at the sidewalk Vivace at 321 Broadway E, between Harrison and Thomas.

listings.name: Macrina Cafe & Bakery
listings.content: A premier local bakery whose chef was a finalist for a 2007 James Beard Award. Selection changes seasonally and daily, but there's always something delicious on offer. An excellent choice for a breakfast or light lunch; cafe-style seating encourages you to sit down and stay a while. Espresso can be inconsistent, if you're picky, grab food to go and walk elsewhere for coffee.

listings.name: Realfine Coffee
listings.content: Social coffee-drinking environment.

listings.name: Broadcast Coffee Roasters
listings.content: A neighborhood shop serving Stumptown coffee and pastries from Alki Bakery. Free WiFi. Great for meetings.

listings.name: Top Pot Doughnuts
listings.content: Nestled into the neighborhood and a favorite weekend hang-out for locals. Incredible doughnuts (try the feather boa doughnut!) in a very Seattle-y atmosphere. Drip coffee isn't so hot, but the freshly-brewed options are all good.

listings.name: Victrola
listings.content: Neighborhood place, more spacious than most. Their roastery also has a (smaller) space at 310 E Pike St in Downtown.

listings.name: Cha Cha Lounge
listings.content: A weird cross of dive bar and trendy spot, the ambiance of their old location was successfully transplanted to this location after their former building was razed for yet more condo construction. Your bartender may have had an album in the charts circa 1992.

listings.name: Pine Box
listings.content: Located in a former funeral home (rumored to have handled Bruce Lee's body) that has now been converted to offices and a beer bar. Enjoy one of the best beer selections in the neighborhood.

listings.name: DeLuxe Bar and Grill
listings.content: Dark, but appealing for a beer, stiff drink or bar food (hearty burgers, thick fries, etc.) More restaurant than bar.

listings.name: Garage
listings.content: A trendy billiards hall and bowling alley, built in a spacious former garage that has no problem handling large groups. Multiple bars with food service, and an outdoor patio (weather permitting).

listings.name: Herb & Bitter Public House
listings.content: An excellent spot for their gourmet and slightly modernist food, but even better for their ever-changing cocktails, expertly designed using seasonal flavors and uncommon ingredients. A patio in the back with a sliding glass roof means you can enjoy the sky view (boxed in by surrounding buildings) rain or shine.

listings.name: Liberty
listings.content: Free WiFi, large couches, decent sushi, good drinks and attractive servers conspire to make this one of the better Capitol Hill bars.

listings.name: Linda's Tavern
listings.content: The outdoor patio makes this the perfect place to enjoy a few drinks under the stars.

listings.name: Smith
listings.content: Another bar owned by Linda Derschang of Linda's fame. Although Smith regularly becomes packed in the evening, large communal tables in the center of the establishment mean you can usually find a place to sit.

listings.name: Stumbling Monk
listings.content: Its dark appearance from the outside makes it easy to miss, but worth stepping inside. As the name suggests, you’ll find an excellent selection of Belgian beer strong enough to make your walk home a challenge. The Stumbling Monk’s unpretentious atmosphere makes it a down-to-earth oasis on trendy Capitol Hill.

listings.name: Summit Public House
listings.content: Offers many beers on tap and is home to one of the best BLTs in the city.

listings.name: Rhein Haus
listings.content: Bavarian beer garden with indoor bocce courts, bratwurst and pretzels.

listings.name: CC's Seattle
listings.content: Dark laid-back bar for all types of men, serving strong drinks. Very community oriented; recurring events fill the bar with a big crowd, such as weekly video game nights on Wednesdays, meetups for leather, furry, or nudist groups, and monthly dances with dress codes such as fetish gear or underwear.

listings.name: Crescent Lounge
listings.content: Small dive bar with nightly karaoke.

listings.name: The Cuff Complex
listings.content: Gay bar and dance club, often attracts a leather crowd.

listings.name: Diesel
listings.content: Bear and cub bar.

listings.name: Madison Pub
listings.content: Unpretentious and crowded gay sports bar. Pool tables and darts.

listings.name: Neighbors
listings.content: Gay dance club. The place to take your straight friends.

listings.name: The Pony
listings.content: Small dive bar in an old building with a year-round patio and fire pit. Wide variety of music, and a schedule full of go-go dancers, karaoke, and tea dancing.

listings.name: Queer/Bar
listings.content: Inclusive bar with a variety of quality performances, and excellent pub food.

listings.name: Seattle Eagle
listings.content: Classic gay leather bar. Underwear parties on Saturdays.

listings.name: Wildrose
listings.content: One of the oldest lesbian bars on the West Coast. Very cheap tacos and Tecates on Tuesdays, and cheap well drinks on Thursdays.

listings.name: Gaslight Inn
listings.content: Bed and breakfast.

listings.name: Silver Cloud Hotel Seattle – Broadway
listings.content: A local chain brand. Rooms are generously spacious. Complete facilities such as complimentary Wi-Fi, a restaurant, gym and swimming pool, which considering the typical price, is a giveaway.

listings.name: Hotel Sorrento
listings.content: This historic hotel has crowned the First Hill since 1908. It is a posh, Italianate, 7-story hotel with fine dining in the AAA - 4 diamond Hunt Club - For a classy night out before the "hopera".

listings.name: Olympic Sculpture Park
listings.content: 9 of green space on Seattle’s waterfront with a collection of monumental sculptures.

listings.name: Seattle Art Museum
listings.content: The museum displays a good assortment of art from the Pacific Northwest and around the world. Though the permanent exhibitions only occasionally delve deeply into a specific subject (such as the enormous variety of pieces in the porcelain room), extensive special exhibitions fill the gap. Tours available.
listings.price: Suggested admission: $19.50 adult, $17.50 senior/military, $2.50 students/youth, children 12 and under free. Admission is free on first Thursday of the month

listings.name: Seattle Public Library-Central Library
listings.content: A dramatic glass and steel structure in the heart of Downtown, designed by Rem Koolhaas. This is not an average public library and has become a tourist destination in its own right. A popular way to experience the unique architecture of the building is to take an elevator to the 10th floor, the highest observation deck in the building. From here you can walk down to the main floor through the Book Spiral; the core of the structure which organizes the library's books in one continuous path organized by the Dewey decimal system.

listings.name: Sky View Observatory
listings.content: This observatory sits on the 73rd floor of the Columbia Center, one of the tallest buildings on the West Coast and the tallest public observation deck in the Pacific Northwest, sitting 932 feet (284.2 meters) above the ground and more than 330 feet taller than the Space Needle. Great views are offered from the top and some people claim the view is better from here than from the Space Needle. Another advantage over the Space Needle is that this building isn't well known as a tourist attraction, so there's usually little to no line to get to the top. Tickets are available for purchase online ($2 less expensive or in the atrium at the Columbia Center). There is a cafe in the observation deck serving sandwiches and drinks (including beer and wine) and a food court at the bottom of the Columbia Center.
listings.price: $22 adults, $19 seniors and military with ID, $16.for kids 5 to 13

listings.name: Tilikum Place
listings.content: Etymologically meaning "welcome" in the native Chinook language, Tilikum is home to a statue of Chief Seattle, the chief of the Duwamish tribe that gives this city its name. Sit in the park or in the Tilikum Place Cafe's outdoor seating and enjoy views of the Space Needle while sipping a coffee or enjoying a lunch, and watch the monorail go by.

listings.name: Miner's Landing at Pier 57
listings.content: Named for once being the main departure point during the Seattle gold rush, Miner's Landing now hosts a food court and a variety of gourmet restaurants, a sports merchandise store, a carousel for kids and the Seattle Great Wheel.

listings.name: Seattle Great Wheel
listings.content: Rising 175 feet in the air, this Ferris wheel offers a 15-minute ride in one of the wheel's 42 gondolas, each of which can hold up to 8 people. You'll get a wonderful view of the Seattle waterfront, the Downtown skyline, as well as the Puget Sound, the snow-covered Olympics, and the green city hills.

listings.name: Seattle Aquarium
listings.content: Showcases native fish and mammals of the Pacific Northwest. Among the highlights are the Windows on Washington (WOW) exhibit, two touch tanks featuring animals of the inland sea and outer coast, and a display that holds two giant pacific octopuses, gill sharks and Pacific coral reefs. The outdoor exhibit upstairs features a collection of birds, harbor and Northern fur seals, as well as river and sea otters. At a separate area on the lower level, you can go inside an underwater dome to get up-close with swimming animals from the Puget Sound.
listings.price: $21.95 adults, $14.95 children (4-12), children 3 and under free
listings.address: 1483 Alaskan Way (on Pier 59 on the waterfront)

listings.name: Argosy Cruises
listings.content: Offers special dinner and sightseeing cruises. The most common tour visitors take is the hour-long journey on Elliott Bay, which gives you an excellent view not just of the Space Needle and the Downtown skyline, but the freight harbor to the south as well.
listings.price: Prices vary according to your itinerary; $23.75 for harbor cruise

listings.name: Seattle Convention Center
listings.content: The largest events space in the state, and the host of PAX West, Emerald City Comic Con, Sakura-Con, the Northwest Flower and Garden Show, and many others. The 414,722 Arch building spans across Pike Street, 8th Avenue, and I-5. The 573,770 Summit building, opened in 2023, is a block north.

listings.name: Benaroya Hall
listings.content: An aesthetically and acoustically beautiful new concert hall. The official home of the Seattle Symphony Orchestra, it also houses other classical and performing arts roadshows.

listings.name: 5th Avenue Theatre
listings.content: The main Seattle venue for touring Broadway musical shows; also hosts a number of original musicals that later head to Broadway.

listings.name: Unexpected Productions
listings.content: Seattle's longest running improv theater.

listings.name: Seattle International Film Festival (SIFF)
listings.content: One of the largest film festivals in North America. Screenings are at the SIFF Cinema Uptown (3 screens), the SIFF Cinema Downtown, and two venues at Seattle Center, the SIFF Film Center and the PACCAR IMAX Theater.

listings.name: SIFF Cinema Downtown
listings.content: One of just three Cinerama theaters in the world, this cinema shows art, indie, and foreign films and documentaries.

listings.name: The 5 Point Cafe
listings.content: Seattle's oldest restaurant, serving huge portions of American comfort food since 1929. The full menu is served 24 hours every day. Full bar with stiff drinks, over 25 local beers and liquors. Great jukebox and an eclectic mix of regulars and locals, tourists, politicians, young hipsters, freaks and grouchy old men. Free wifi. Outdoor seating. This is a true piece of Seattle history not to be missed.

listings.name: Biscuit Bitch
listings.content: The b-word is in every single item on the menu, and this excellent breakfast place is a siren call to those seeking hangover relief, providing burgers (replace the bun with a biscuit) sandwiches (replace the bread with a biscuit), and typical Southern style food.

listings.name: Ivar's Acres Of Clams
listings.content: Smoked salmon plate-lunch and fish-n-chips served outdoors at a scenic waterfront location. Ordering at the walk-up counter outside is inexpensive. Please do not feed ducks and seagulls as human food is harmful for birds! Good food, but pretty touristy.

listings.name: Beecher's Handmade Cheese
listings.content: A library of artisan cheese from Pacific Northwest farms, as well as some handmade cheese in the factory next door, worth bringing home as a Seattle souvenir. Try some free samples and be sure to get some of their mac and cheese.
listings.price: Prices per cheese vary, but a piece weighing 0.5 lb generally costs $10

listings.name: The Crumpet Shop
listings.content: Get a crumpet, a griddle cake originated from England, made with organic ingredients, sweet or savory with a number of toppings.

listings.name: Ellenos Greek Yogurt
listings.content: A bit expensive compared to its supermarket counterparts, but richer in flavor and milk, making this a local favorite. Often has long lines, but they move quickly and the owner is generous with free samples.

listings.name: Jack's Fish Spot
listings.content: A good place to get seafood, especially dungeness crabs. Market-like atmosphere, seating in stools, and they can cook what you buy.

listings.name: Pike Place Chowder
listings.content: One of the most famous restaurants at Pike Place Market. Selections of exceptional chowder, as well as sandwiches and seafood cocktails.

listings.name: Pike Place Chowder
listings.content: Usually has long lines (up to 30 minutes) due to the fact this location is more well-known. Has more choices of chowder. Seats quickly fill up!

listings.name: Piroshky Piroshky
listings.content: A very popular eatery, specializing in their namesake Russian pastries. They have many varieties from which to choose. The smoked salmon, the cheese, onion and garlic roll, and the apple cinnamon roll are all excellent. Be prepared for long lines and out of stock items if you come in late!

listings.name: Cafe Campagne
listings.content: Country French cuisine.

listings.name: Matt's in the Market
listings.content: Charming market ambiance and tasty seafood selections make for a fine low-key dining experience at this small spot.

listings.name: Palace Kitchen
listings.content: Tom Douglas' upscale saloon is a hit any time of day.

listings.name: Serious Pie
listings.content: Regular and specialty Neapolitan style pizza in one of the best pizza restaurants in Seattle. This small space gets overwhelmed with customers around mealtimes.

listings.name: Le Pichet
listings.content: An excellent French bistro. Try the roast chicken.

listings.name: Ruth's Chris Steakhouse
listings.content: Side dishes served on a per-table basis, so make sure you can agree with your companions! Skip the happy hour.

listings.name: The Metropolitan Grill
listings.content: Caters to those with fat wallets, with massive portions, classic steakhouse ambiance, and top-grade beef.

listings.name: Purple Cafe & Wine Bar
listings.content: Has an extensive wine list and some of Seattle's best food. Don't forget to try the salted caramels for dessert.

listings.name: Elliott's Oyster House
listings.content: Seafood restaurant that's most famous for fresh oysters. In addition, the menu has various seafood to choose from, such as king salmon, sockeye, dungeness crab, king crab, yellowfin ahi tuna, you name it. Happy hour is affordable, with chef's choice of fresh oysters and other deals. The restaurant is right by the dock and the view is fantastic during the summer when you can sit outside.

listings.name: Cyclops
listings.content: Good, hip (but not ultra-hip) bar, and not a bad restaurant either. Interesting neo-retro decor. The Ace Hotel is upstairs. Excellent breakfast.

listings.name: Owl N' Thistle
listings.content: A great Irish bar. A house band, nice regulars, and halibut burger to die for. Happy hour is M-F 3-7PM.

listings.name: The Pink Door
listings.content: Reasonably good Italian restaurant, but it's a better bar, with a rather romantic European market ambiance and a trellis-covered outdoor deck. Occasional cabaret-style live entertainment, no cover.

listings.name: Shorty's
listings.content: Classic pinball games and Coney Island hot dogs, decorated with creepy clowns. Be sure to check out the Trophy Lounge hidden in the back.

listings.name: Diller's Room
listings.content: Classic cocktail bar with a historic vibe and extensive drink selection. Happy hour is from 4PM to 6PM with $1 off drinks and $12 pizza.

listings.name: Original Starbucks
listings.content: Who would have thought, when this unassuming place opened in 1971, that it would give rise to a global empire? Now flocks of tourists crowd the oldest existing Starbucks. (The true first location was one block north; it moved here when that building was torn down in 1977.) The long line gets you exactly the same drinks you can get at every other location. If you're not a true fan, check out the bare-chested mermaid which acted as the original logo for the company, then try any of the hundreds of other local Seattle coffee shops.

listings.name: Ace Hotel
listings.content: Budget hotel in the Belltown area. Rooms have an option of shared bath. Minimum furniture and quaint.
listings.price: Shared bath rooms from $120, deluxe from $200

listings.name: City Hostel Seattle
listings.content: Warm friendly accommodation. Private room available. Free breakfast and Wi-fi. All rooms have murals painted by local artists. $25 dorms.

listings.name: Green Tortoise Hostel
listings.content: Has a view of the Puget Sound and the Market, 30 bunk rooms in the elegantly restored Elliot Hotel Building. Free Internet stations and Wi-Fi, free dinner 3 nights a week, and free breakfast every morning. The Green Tortoise is a Seattle backpacker institution that also runs festive low-budget bus tours to Mexico and Central America.

listings.name: Hotel Five Seattle
listings.content: Its namesake comes from the site of the hotel at Fifth Avenue, below the monorail tracks. Urban-designed rooms. Complimentary shuttle and bike to roam the city.

listings.name: La Quinta Inn & Suites Seattle Downtown
listings.content: Very close to Seattle Center and the downtown shopping core. High-speed internet in rooms and free breakfast included.

listings.name: Belltown Inn
listings.content: This little establishment at the heart of Belltown offers kitchenette on every room. Rooms only have fans for summer.

listings.name: Executive Hotel Pacific
listings.content: A small hotel in the Belltown area. Standard rooms have small bathrooms, deluxe are slightly larger, suites' bedrooms are perfect for a family and features free Internet and newspaper.

listings.name: Hotel Max
listings.content: In the heart of downtown, offers an artistic setting for both business and leisure travelers.

listings.name: Mayflower Park Hotel
listings.content: Built in 1927, the centrally-located hotel retains its classical colors on most of its interior, with modern amenities in the rooms such as flat-screen TV and coffee machine. Wi-Fi is complimentary.

listings.name: Palladian Hotel
listings.content: A boutique hotel, developed by Kimpton, adopts a European flair. Every room is equipped with a yoga mat and a daily social (wine) hour is available at the hotel's classic bar.

listings.name: Renaissance Seattle Hotel
listings.content: A full service hotel in the heart of downtown.

listings.name: The Roosevelt Hotel
listings.content: Another boutique and historic option at Belltown.

listings.name: Warwick Seattle
listings.content: One of the few budget options in the middle of downtown. Rooms have a view of either the skyline or the Space Needle, added with a Juliet balcony.

listings.name: The Alexis Royal Sonesta Hotel Seattle
listings.content: This art-themed hotel has original works throughout the lobby and in the rooms. Furthermore, it sports a big old Dale Chihuly glass piece in the lobby.

listings.name: The Edgewater
listings.content: Near the Pike Place Market, right on the water, and famous for three things: you could at one time literally fish right out of your window, it was the site of a notorious Led Zeppelin incident, and the Beatles stayed here during their 1964 tour. Rooms either face the city with no great view other than the Space Needle, or face the water. These latter rooms enjoy the non-stop action of the ferries and cruise liners in the harbor. The restaurant is elegantly decorated with a few outdoor tables right over the water.

listings.name: The Fairmont Olympic
listings.content: The only hotel in the Northwest to win a five-diamond award. Pulls off grand and luxurious perfectly, is in the middle of downtown.

listings.name: Hilton Motif Seattle
listings.content: Distinctive downtown hotel featuring modern lifestyle amenities, concierge, restaurants and lounges, meeting venues, business & fitness centers, and Seattle's largest rooftop dining patio - a unique Seattle Lodging experience.

listings.name: Hotel 1000
listings.content: New high-tech, boutique style hotel in downtown.

listings.name: Hotel Andra
listings.content: A hotel of a local brand with a luxury and modern touch. Rooms have private bars and ironing boards, with plush Turkish towels and Swedish bath amenities. The in-house Mediterranean restaurant is managed by the locally-renowned restaurateur Tom Douglas.

listings.name: Hotel Monaco Seattle
listings.content: Centrally located in the historic Pike Place Market downtown, facing the waterfront and Elliott Bay. Short walk to Seattle Art Museum, Benaroya Hall, Pioneer Square, Westlake Center, and lots of dining and shopping.

listings.name: Pan Pacific Hotel Seattle
listings.content: This pet-friendly property offers an array of luxury fully furnished rooms and suites equipped with all modern amenities. Facilities include a business center and a fitness center.

listings.name: Sheraton Grand Seattle
listings.content: Immediately adjacent to the convention center.

listings.name: W Seattle
listings.content: For the terminally hip traveler. Decorated in a stunning palette of black, black, silver, cream, and black.

listings.name: The Westin Seattle
listings.content: Perhaps the hotel that has the most rooms in the city. Standard luxurious Westin-style hospitality. It is linked by a skybridge that connects with Westlake Center.

listings.name: Fremont Bridge
listings.content: A bascule bridge (drawbridge) spanning the Fremont Cut since 1917. The bridge opens an average of 35 times a day, which makes it the most frequently opened drawbridge in the United States and one of the busiest bascule bridges in the world.

listings.name: Gas Works Park
listings.content: "Gasworks" is Wallingford's oddly endearing refuge along the north part of Lake Union — prominently featuring the rusting, hulking remains of the city's old gasworks piping and machinery. More conventionally, a solitary bump of a hill offers the ideal spot for kite flying and views across the lake of sailboats, float planes landing, and downtown Seattle at sunset. Generally quiet but exceptionally crowded during the 4th of July for firework shows.

listings.name: Woodland Park
listings.content: One of the city's most active hubs for sports and recreation, including walkway paths, several playfields, tennis courts, lawn bowling, horseshoe pits, a skatepark, and a large, wooded dog off-leash area.

listings.name: Woodland Park Zoo
listings.content: The zoo hosts 1,100 animals from 300 different species, each housed in nice, naturalistic exhibits. You can feed a giraffe or an elephant by yourself for $5, or enter the aviary where the birds fly overhead and show off talents with the aid of a zookeeper. For the kids, the zoomazium is an additional place to visit for slides and a century-old carousel. Allow at least 3 hours of your time to fully explore the zoo.
listings.price: May–September $18.75 per adult, $11.75 per child; October–May $11.75 per adult, $8.75 per child. Discounts for using public transit or on a rainy day!

listings.name: Waiting for the Interurban
listings.content: A statue of five people (and a dog) waiting for the trolley that has not existed since the 1930s. The statue is frequently clothed by local residents. There was a time when this work was considered offbeat (imagine that!).
listings.address: N. 34th St. at Fremont Ave., at the north approach to the Fremont Bridge

listings.name: Fremont Rocket
listings.content: A 53' Cold War rocket, improved with neon space blasters and a smoke generator in the engine bay, towers over the corner of N. 35th Street and Evanston Avenue.

listings.name: Fremont Troll
listings.content: Strikingly large (photos generally don't do it justice), the Troll is a concrete statue under the Aurora Bridge clutching a full size Volkswagen Bug in its grip. The statue is notable enough to even gets its own street name - just off of N. 36th Street on Troll Avenue.

listings.name: Statue of Lenin
listings.content: This bronze statue peers out over the street below, oblivious to the continuing controversy over its display. It was salvaged and brought over from Slovakia and was re-erected in 1995 in a Fremont parking lot that at the time hosted a weekly market before being moved a few years later to its current site.

listings.name: Tai Chi at Meridian Park
listings.content: On most Sunday mornings, groups of people practice tai chi or assorted other martial arts in the southeast quadrant of Meridian Park.

listings.name: Fremont Abbey Arts Center
listings.content: A performing and demonstrative arts venue.

listings.name: Fremont Fair
listings.content: If you happen to be in Seattle around the Summer Solstice, Fremont hosts one of the city's best street fairs on the weekend closest to the solstice. The highlight is the Solstice Parade on Saturday afternoon, an arts-only parade held by the Fremont Art's Council with hundreds, perhaps even thousands, of elaborately costumed participants, no signage (strongly discouraging commercial participation), and only human-powered floats. A contingent of nude and painted bicyclists traditionally show up and ride before the parade begins. Delilah's "Billion Belly March" contingent annually brings over a hundred belly dancers and drummers to the parade.

listings.name: Fremont Oktoberfest
listings.content: An annual microbrew tasting event that features the Texas Chainsaw Pumpkin Carving Contest, live music, three beer gardens, a dog day event, the Brew HA-HA 5K, a comedy show, and the Miss Buxom Contest.
listings.price: From $15 if purchased in advance, $20 same day

listings.name: Dick's Drive-In
listings.content: This is a local legend of a drive-in/drive-out burger joint which has served the dual purpose of providing a gathering place for high school and UW students before and after sporting events.

listings.name: Paseo Caribbean Restaurant
listings.content: A tiny Cuban restaurant with amazing sandwiches like a crunchy baguette slathered with a secret aioli and filled with your choice of protein (the most popular is the roasted pork shoulder), fresh cilantro, pickled jalapeños, lettuce and delicious caramelized onions. A local favorite, it's best to call ahead and place your order. Expect to settle for takeout; the 3 tables are usually full but there are several nearby parks you can stroll to, as well as the main section of Fremont. They do run out of sandwiches late in the day, but other wonderful entrees are served.

listings.name: The Dish
listings.content: New American cuisine. Home of the Slacker Special: scrambled eggs or tofu, cheese, tortilla chips, enchilada sauce and sour cream served with potatoes and toast. Although you might see a line outside, it never takes long to be seated and it's worth the wait.

listings.name: Musashi's
listings.content: A small hole-in-the-wall Japanese eatery that attracts crowds of patrons waiting for a bowl of sushi rice with assorted sashimi (called chirashi), which is not listed on the menu. Opens for lunch and dinner only. Cheap for its portion sizes.

listings.name: Ivar's Salmon House
listings.content: Various seafood entrees served in a neo-longhouse replete with totem poles and various other carved cedar adornments. Ivar's has an excellent and affordable happy hour menu (7 days a week 3:30PM-6:30PM and 9PM-close) that many locals and University of Washington staff and faculty enjoy regularly. The thing to get is salmon smoked to order over the big wood fire in the northwest style.

listings.name: TangleTown Public House
listings.content: Pub and patio where pizza is popular fare.

listings.name: George and Dragon
listings.content: British style pub with pretty standard dark wood interior. Great for watching soccer games.

listings.name: Murphy's Pub
listings.content: Irish pub with a good selection of drinks, fair pub food. Attracts a young and educated crowd. Trivia on Tuesday evenings.

listings.name: Sea Monster Lounge
listings.content: Decent selection of beer, cocktails, and wine. Fresh sushi made onsite with sake. Free live music every night.

listings.name: Zoka Coffee
listings.content: In what is variously known as the Meridian District or Tangletown, between Wallingford and Green Lake. Hip students, professionals, and soccer moms meet here. Great desserts and whole grain scones. Roasts their own coffee, supplying to cafes across the U.S. and at Zoka's two cafes in Japan. There is also one north of the U-Village shopping complex on Blakely.

listings.name: Fremont Brewing
listings.content: Local brewery with large outdoor beer garden (Urban Beer Garden) as well as an indoor area. Has a wide area of beer available for pickup as well as dine-in.

listings.name: Hotel Hotel
listings.content: European style hotel/hostel in the heart of Fremont.
